summary: A response to RFC 606 about providing Host names on-line, one of several related notes with RFCs 623, 625 and 627. It was replaced by RFC 810.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 608 agrees with a proposal for the NIC to provide an online ASCII file listing host names, addresses, and status. It describes the initial entry format and proposed FTP access; RFC 810 later obsoleted this memo.

questions: what was the nics host list
how did early networks find host addresses
what did rfc 608 propose for host names
subtitle: A proposal for an online, machine-readable file of host names and addresses.

tldr.problem: Network users needed an accessible way to look up official host names, network-relative addresses, and basic host status information.
tldr.mechanism: The NIC proposed generating an ASCII host file from a maintained source file and making it available through FTP.
tldr.outcome: RFC 608 responded to RFC 606 and was obsoleted by RFC 810.

sections.title: A Shared List of Hosts
sections.content:
The NIC agrees with the proposal in RFC 606 to maintain an online ASCII text file of host names, addresses, and attributes. The NIC already had a source file in NLS format and proposed writing a program to generate an updated ASCII file from it periodically.

The source data included official host names, host addresses, host status, technical liaisons, host computers, and operating systems. At first, the generated list would include only the basic host entry and a STATUS attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC proposed keeping one source list and generating a readable text file from it. The file would make basic host details available in one place.

sections.title: Host Entries and Status
sections.content:
The proposed basic entry contains a host name and a decimal host address relative to the host's own network. A host name may contain up to 48 characters from letters, digits, and hyphens; it must start with a letter and cannot end with a hyphen. For hosts outside the ARPANET, an official network name of up to 24 characters may prefix the host name in parentheses.

The initial STATUS attribute can be SERVER, USER, TIP, or UNKNOWN. The memo lists other possible attributes, such as nicknames, FTP byte sizes, and echoing behavior, but says those details were not yet in the source file.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry gives a host name, a network-relative address, and an initial status label. Other details were suggested for later but were not part of the first list.

sections.title: Proposed File Access
sections.content: The ASCII file was to be stored on host OFFICE-1, whose host address the RFC gives as 43 decimal, at <NETINFO>HOSTS.TXT. The memo says anyone could retrieve it using FTP with the listed guest login values. Entries would be in alphanumeric order by host name, and availability would be announced when the file was ready.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal placed the file on OFFICE-1 for retrieval with FTP. It would be sorted by host name, and a later announcement would tell readers when it was ready.

references.text: Deutsch, P., "Specification of Internetwork Naming Units", RFC 606, January 1974.
